name: How the Web Works
author: Recurse
subject: web
description: From URL and DNS through TCP, TLS and HTTP to cookies, caching and CORS, and what happens when you type a URL.

lesson.intro: Opening a page runs a precise sequence: parse a URL, look up an IP address, open an encrypted connection, exchange HTTP messages, send cookies and reuse cached files. Knowing it lets you debug API calls, speed up pages and ace a classic interview question.
objectives: Break a URL into its parts and explain how DNS finds the IP address
Describe the TCP and TLS handshakes and what HTTPS protects
Read HTTP requests and responses, choosing methods and status codes
Explain cookies, sessions, tokens and caching headers
Walk through everything that happens when you press Enter on a URL

sections.title: Anatomy of a URL
sections.key: A URL names the scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment; scheme, host and port together form the origin, and the fragment never reaches the server.
sections.body:
Every web request starts with a URL, and each part means something. Take `https://shop.example.com:8443/search?q=red+shoes&page=2#reviews`:

[[visual]]

Other characters are **percent-encoded**: a space becomes `%20` (or `+` in a query), and `&` inside a value becomes `%26`. Build URLs with `URLSearchParams` or `urllib.parse.urlencode`, not by gluing strings, or a value containing `&` splits into two parameters.

The **origin** is scheme, host and port together. Browsers use it to decide which pages may read each other's data, so it returns with cookies and CORS.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Six parts of a URL
rows: Protocol: HTTP over TLS (`http` is unencrypted)
The name DNS turns into an IP address
Which service. Defaults: 443 for https, 80 for http
`key=value` pairs joined by `&`: searches, filters, pages
A spot in the page. Never sent to the server

sections.pitfall: Assuming the fragment reaches the server. Anything after `#` stays in the browser; data the server needs belongs in the path or the query string.

check.question: In `https://api.example.com/v1/users?limit=10#top`, what is the query string?
choices: /v1/users
top
limit=10
api.example.com
check.explanation: The query string is everything between ? and #. /v1/users is the path, top is the fragment and api.example.com is the host.

sections.title: DNS: from name to IP address
sections.key: DNS turns names into IP addresses through cached, layered lookups: caches first, then a resolver that walks from the root to the TLD to the authoritative server.
sections.body:
Computers connect to IP addresses like `203.0.113.10`, not names. The **Domain Name System** (DNS) translates one into the other before almost every connection. The browser and the operating system check their caches (and the OS its `hosts` file) first; a hit ends the lookup.

[[visual]]

Every answer carries a **TTL** (time to live, in seconds): how long it may be cached. Caching makes most lookups take a millisecond or two, but changes spread slowly: after you move a site, some users reach the old server until their cached answer expires.

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

visual.title: Record types
rows: An alias to another name: `www.example.com` to `example.com`
The mail servers for the domain
Free text: domain verification, email anti-spoofing rules

sections.code:
$ dig shop.example.com +noall +answer
shop.example.com. 300 IN A 203.0.113.10

$ dig www.example.com +noall +answer
www.example.com. 3600 IN CNAME example.com.
example.com.     300  IN A     203.0.113.20
sections.deeper:
The columns of a dig answer are name, TTL, class, type and value.

Lowering a record's TTL a day before a migration means caches let go of the old answer quickly when you switch.

Classic DNS travels unencrypted over UDP port 53, so anyone on your network can see which names you look up; DNS over HTTPS (DoH) encrypts those queries. `nslookup` is the older alternative to `dig`.
sections.pitfall: Changing a DNS record and expecting every user to see it at once. Resolvers keep the old answer until its TTL runs out, so plan changes around the TTL.

check.question: Why does a DNS lookup for a popular site often take only a millisecond or two?
choices: DNS servers are usually located inside your own building
Popular sites skip DNS and connect by name instead
The root servers keep a copy of every website
The answer is usually already cached by the browser, OS or resolver
check.explanation: Each layer caches answers for their TTL, so most lookups never leave your machine or your resolver. The full walk from root to authoritative server happens only on a cold cache.

sections.title: TCP and TLS: opening a secure connection
sections.key: Before any HTTP, TCP opens a reliable byte stream with a three-way handshake, then TLS checks the server's certificate and agrees on keys; HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS.
sections.body:
With an IP address in hand, the browser still needs a reliable, encrypted channel.

**TCP** turns a network that loses, duplicates and reorders packets into a reliable, ordered byte stream between two ports; the server listens on 443 (80 for plain HTTP). Every chunk is numbered and acknowledged, and lost data is resent, so HTTP never thinks about lost packets.

[[visual]]

The browser checks the **certificate**: it must chain to a trusted certificate authority (CA), be within its dates and name the exact host. Both sides then derive the same session keys, which never cross the network.

[[visual 2]]

messages.label: ClientHello + key share
messages.detail: TLS versions and ciphers it supports

visual.title: What HTTPS does and does not do

items.title: Protects
points: Hides the path, query string, headers, cookies and body
Stops anyone on the network altering the page
Stops impersonation, as long as the certificate is checked

items.title: Does not
points: Hide the hostname, usually: DNS and the TLS hello leak it
Prove the site is honest: a phishing site can hold a valid certificate for its own lookalike domain

sections.deeper:
Newer HTTP versions cut the setup cost. HTTP/1.1 keeps a connection open for several requests in a row, HTTP/2 runs many requests in parallel over one connection, and HTTP/3 runs over **QUIC**, a UDP-based transport that merges the transport and TLS handshakes into one.

A certificate proves only that the server controls the domain, as vouched for by a CA the browser trusts. Any failed check produces a full-page browser warning.
sections.pitfall: Treating the padlock as proof that a site is trustworthy. It means only that your connection to that domain is encrypted; check that the domain is the one you meant.

activity.title: Handshake and a lost segment
activity.prompt: Step through the handshake, then the lost segment. Notice the work TCP does that HTTP never sees: sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission. Finish with the UDP comparison and think about why HTTP/3 builds on UDP and adds its own reliability on top.

check.question: Why does TCP number and acknowledge every chunk of data it sends?
choices: So each chunk can be encrypted with a different key
So lost or out-of-order data can be detected, resent and reassembled
So DNS can choose a faster route for the next chunk
So the server can tell which browser sent the data
check.explanation: Sequence numbers let the receiver put data back in order and spot gaps, and acknowledgments tell the sender what arrived. Anything unacknowledged is retransmitted. Encryption is TLS's job, not TCP's.

sections.title: Requests, methods and REST
sections.key: A request is a method, a path, headers and an optional body; the method says what to do, and only safe or idempotent requests can be retried freely.
sections.body:
HTTP is request-response: the client sends one request and gets exactly one response. HTTP/1.1 is readable text; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 encode the same meaning in binary frames. With curl, `-X` sets the method, `-H` adds a header and `-d` sends a body:

[[code]]

`Host` names the site, `Content-Type` the body's format, `Accept` the formats wanted back, and `Authorization` carries credentials.

[[visual]]

A **safe** method changes nothing, so browsers, crawlers and caches send it freely. An **idempotent** one has the same effect once or five times: a client can retry a failed PUT, but a retried POST may create two orders.

**REST** names resources with nouns and lets the method be the verb: `PATCH /users/42`, not `POST /updateUser?id=42`.

visual.title: Methods
rows: Reads a resource. No body, no changes
Creates something, or triggers a process
GET without the body; what is allowed

sections.code:
$ curl -v https://api.example.com/tasks \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"title": "Practice REST"}'
> POST /tasks HTTP/1.1
> Host: api.example.com
> Accept: */*
> Content-Type: application/json
> Content-Length: 26
>
< HTTP/1.1 201 Created
...
sections.pitfall: Changing data with a GET request, such as `GET /deleteUser?id=7`. Browsers prefetch links, crawlers follow them and caches replay them, so a GET must have no side effects.

activity.title: CRUD with a REST API
activity.prompt: Work through the tasks in order. For every response, read the status line and headers before the body: notice the 201 and its Location header after the POST, and the 204 with an empty body after the DELETE.

check.question: A payment request timed out and the client cannot tell whether it went through. Why is retrying a POST riskier than retrying a PUT?
choices: POST is not idempotent, so a retry might charge the customer twice
POST requests are never allowed to be sent more than once
PUT requests are encrypted, while POST requests are not
POST bodies are lost whenever the connection times out
check.explanation: Repeating a PUT just sets the same state again, but each POST may create a new charge. Payment APIs add an idempotency key header so the server can recognize a retry of the same request.

sections.title: Responses: status codes and headers
sections.key: A status code's first digit says whose problem it is: 2xx success, 3xx look elsewhere, 4xx the request was wrong, 5xx the server failed.
sections.body:
Every response starts with a status line such as `HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found`, then headers, a blank line and the body. Read the status first when debugging.

[[visual]]

Headers describe the body and give instructions: `Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, `Location`, `Set-Cookie`, `Cache-Control`, `ETag`.

In JavaScript, `fetch` rejects only when the network fails. A 404 or 500 still resolves, so check `res.ok`:

[[code]]

**CORS**: browsers stop a page's JavaScript from reading another origin's responses unless the server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. For a JSON `PUT` with `Authorization`, the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` **preflight**. Only browsers enforce CORS, so curl still works.

visual.title: Status codes
rows: Usually with a `Location` naming the new resource
Success, empty body; common after DELETE
Moved permanently, found: go to the `Location` header
Your cached copy is still good
Not found; method not allowed on this path
A crash or bug in the app
A proxy or load balancer got no good answer from the app: wait and retry

sections.pitfall: Returning 200 with an error message in the body. Clients, monitoring and retry logic rely on the status code, so a failure should use a 4xx or 5xx code.

activity.title: Break it on purpose
activity.prompt: Trigger each error deliberately. Before you send a request, predict the status code, then read the response body for the server's explanation. The 405 and 415 cases are the two people mix up most often.

check.question: An API returns `503 Service Unavailable`. Whose side is the problem on, and what is a sensible client reaction?
choices: The client's side: fix the request body before retrying
The client's side: log in again to get a fresh token
The server's side: wait and retry later, ideally with backoff
The DNS server's side: flush the DNS cache and retry at once
check.explanation: 5xx codes mean the server failed, and 503 specifically signals a temporary condition such as overload or maintenance. Retrying after a delay, with growing gaps between attempts, is the polite fix. Changing the request will not help.

sections.title: Cookies, sessions and tokens
sections.key: HTTP is stateless, so a login sets a cookie holding a random session ID that the browser sends with every request; HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite protect it.
sections.body:
HTTP is **stateless**: each request stands alone. Yet you log in once and stay logged in, thanks to **cookies**: name-value pairs the server stores in the browser with `Set-Cookie`, which the browser then attaches to every request for that site.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

The session ID is effectively your login, so its **attributes** matter:

[[visual 2]]

APIs for mobile and single-page apps often use **tokens** instead: the app sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` itself. Nothing attaches it automatically, which avoids CSRF, but a token in `localStorage` can be read by any injected script.

messages.note: Logout deletes the session, so a copied ID becomes useless

visual.title: Cookie attributes
rows: Page JavaScript cannot read it, so an injected script cannot steal it
Not sent with requests other sites trigger, such as a hidden form posting to your bank: blocks most **CSRF**. `None` allows it and needs Secure
Lifetime; without them it dies with the browser session
Which hosts and paths receive it

sections.code:
$ curl -i https://shop.example.com/login \
    -d "username=ada&password=..."
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /account
Set-Cookie: session=8f2a9c41e7b04d; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=86400
sections.pitfall: Storing user data such as the role or user ID directly in a plain cookie. The user can edit it; keep only a random session ID (or a signed token) and look the data up.

check.question: Why does a session cookie hold a long random ID rather than, say, the username?
choices: Cookies cannot store letters, only numbers and symbols
Users can edit cookies, so the value must be unguessable and meaningless on its own
Random IDs make the cookie smaller than a username would
Browsers refuse cookies that contain readable words
check.explanation: Anyone can change their own cookies. If the cookie said user=ada, changing it to user=admin would work. A random ID only points to session data kept on the server, and guessing someone else's is practically impossible.

sections.title: Caching
sections.key: Cache-Control says how long a copy stays fresh; a stale copy is revalidated with an ETag and a cheap 304, and fingerprinted file names can be cached for a year.
sections.body:
The fastest request is the one never sent. Browsers, CDNs and proxies reuse stored responses, and the server controls this with headers.

[[visual]]

When a copy is stale, the browser **revalidates** it instead of downloading it again:

[[visual 2]]

**Fingerprinted file names** get the best treatment: build tools name files after their content (`app.3f9c2b.js`) and serve them with `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`. A deploy changes the name, so users get updates at once; the HTML itself is `no-cache`.

**CDNs** are shared caches near each user. Never let them cache personal data.

visual.title: Cache-Control
rows: **Fresh** for an hour: reuse it without asking the server
Store it, but **revalidate** before every reuse. The name misleads many people
Never store it: bank statements and other sensitive data
Only the user's own browser may cache it
Shared caches such as CDNs may cache it too

visual.title: Revalidating with an ETag

messages.note: Next visit: the copy is stale

visual.caption: A 304 still costs a round trip but saves the download. `Last-Modified` with `If-Modified-Since` works the same way.

sections.deeper:
An **ETag** is a fingerprint of the content that the server chose; any change to the file gives a new ETag, so a mismatch means "send the new version".

CDNs (content delivery networks) answer cacheable requests from servers near each user, cutting latency and load on your servers. Caching mistakes cut both ways: too little and the site is slow; too much and users see stale pages or, worse, someone else's private data.
sections.pitfall: Marking personalized responses, such as an account page or an API reply with user data, as public. A CDN may then serve one user's data to another; use `private` or `no-store`.

check.question: A stylesheet was served with `Cache-Control: max-age=600`. Two minutes later you open another page that uses the same file. What usually happens?
choices: The browser asks the server and gets a 304
The browser downloads the whole file again
The page waits until the ten minutes have passed
The browser reuses its copy without contacting the server
check.explanation: Within max-age the copy is fresh, so the browser uses it with no request at all. Only after 600 seconds does it become stale and need revalidation, which may then end in a 304.

sections.title: Putting it together: what happens when you type a URL
sections.key: Pressing Enter triggers, in order: parse, DNS, TCP, TLS, the request, server work, the response, then rendering, and caches shorten every step on repeat visits.
sections.body:
"What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?" is a favorite interview question because it touches everything in this lesson. Walk the layers in order, and mention caches on the way:

[[visual]]

The HTML references stylesheets, scripts and images. Each is a **separate request**, often sent in parallel over the same connection, and many come straight from the cache.

The second visit is much faster: the DNS answer is cached, the connection may still be open, and fingerprinted assets need no request at all. Most web performance work trims this list: fewer round trips, smaller files, more cache hits.

steps.label: Parse the input
steps.detail: URL or search? Sites on the HSTS list are upgraded to https first

steps.label: TLS handshake
steps.detail: Certificate checked, keys agreed. HTTP/3's QUIC does both at once over UDP

steps.label: Send GET /
steps.detail: Host, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Encoding and any cookies

steps.label: The server works
steps.detail: A CDN answers from cache, or an app server queries a database and renders HTML

steps.label: Receive the response
steps.detail: Status, headers, compressed HTML. A 301 or 302 restarts at the Location

steps.label: Render
steps.detail: Build the DOM, fetch subresources, lay out, paint, run JavaScript

sections.pitfall: Answering this interview question with a single layer, only DNS or only rendering. Walk the whole path in order, then go deeper wherever the interviewer asks.

check.question: Which step has to finish before the TLS handshake can begin?
choices: The HTTP GET request for the page
The TCP connection to port 443
The browser rendering the HTML
The server sending its cookies
check.explanation: TLS runs on top of an established TCP connection, and the HTTP request travels inside TLS. Rendering and cookies come later still.

keyTerms.definition: A web address: scheme, host, optional port, path, query string and fragment.
The scheme, host and port of a URL together; browsers isolate pages by origin.
The distributed system that translates names like example.com into IP addresses.
How many seconds a DNS answer (or other cached data) may be reused before asking again.
The transport protocol that provides a reliable, ordered byte stream, opened with a three-way handshake.
The protocol that encrypts a connection and verifies the server's certificate; HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.
Having the same effect whether a request is sent once or many times, like GET, PUT and DELETE.
The three-digit result of a request: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
A name-value pair the server sets with Set-Cookie and the browser sends back automatically.
Server-side state about a logged-in user, found through a random ID stored in a cookie.
The header that says whether and for how long a response may be cached and reused.
Response headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin that let pages from other origins read a response.

summary: A URL is scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment; the first three form the origin.
DNS resolves names through layered, cached lookups that honor each TTL.
TCP makes a reliable stream, TLS adds encryption and a certificate check: that is HTTPS.
Methods say what to do; 2xx success, 3xx elsewhere, 4xx bad request, 5xx server failure.
A random session ID in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie keeps you logged in.
Cache-Control, ETags and fingerprinted names skip most requests on repeat visits.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a curious friend what happens between typing shop.example.com into a browser and seeing the page: name each step in order, and say what makes the second visit faster than the first.

questions.question: Type the path part of `https://docs.example.org:8443/guides/setup?lang=en#step-2`.
questions.explanation: The path starts after the host and port and ends where the query string (?lang=en) begins. The query and the fragment (#step-2) are separate parts of the URL.

questions.question: In what order do these steps happen when you first load `https://example.com`?
choices: TCP connect, DNS lookup, HTTP request, TLS handshake
DNS lookup, TCP connect, TLS handshake, HTTP request
HTTP request, DNS lookup, TLS handshake, TCP connect
TLS handshake, DNS lookup, TCP connect, HTTP request
questions.explanation: The browser needs an IP address before it can connect, a TCP connection before it can run TLS, and an encrypted channel before it sends the HTTPS request.

questions.question: The HTML of a page arrives and references one stylesheet, two scripts and five images. What does the browser do next?
choices: Nothing; the server already embedded them in the HTML response
Requests one archive that contains every resource
Repeats the DNS lookup once for each resource
Requests each of those resources separately as it finds them
questions.explanation: HTML only contains references. Each stylesheet, script and image is its own HTTP request, often reusing the open connection, and the DNS answer for the same host is already cached.

questions.question: Which of these methods is NOT idempotent?
choices: PUT
DELETE
POST
GET
questions.explanation: Sending the same POST twice usually creates two things, such as two orders. PUT replaces a resource with the same content each time, and a second DELETE finds nothing more to remove.

questions.question: Which request header tells the server what format the request body is in?
questions.explanation: Content-Type describes the body being sent, for example application/json. Accept is different: it says which formats the client wants back.

questions.question: Complete the curl command so the API knows the body is JSON.
choices: Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Content-Length: json
Authorization: application/json
questions.explanation: Without this header, curl -d labels the body application/x-www-form-urlencoded, and many APIs reject it. Accept would only say what format you want in the response.

questions.question: A logged-in user opens an admin page they are not allowed to see. Which status code fits best?
choices: 401 Unauthorized
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error
403 Forbidden
questions.explanation: 403 means the server knows who you are and refuses anyway. Despite its name, 401 means you are not authenticated yet, so logging in might help.

questions.question: Which status code means a new resource was successfully created?
questions.explanation: 201 Created is the usual reply to a successful POST that creates something, often with a Location header pointing at the new resource.

questions.question: A response carries `Cache-Control: no-cache`. What may the browser do with it?
choices: Never store it, not in memory and not on disk
Store it, but check with the server before each reuse
Reuse it freely for an hour without asking the server
Store it, but only if the status code was 304
questions.explanation: no-cache means "revalidate before using", typically with If-None-Match, which is cheap when the server answers 304. no-store is the directive that forbids storing.

questions.question: This code shows "Saved!" even when the server responds with 500. Why?
choices: await cannot be used inside a try block like this
JSON.stringify throws when the server returns an error
fetch only rejects on network errors, so a 500 still resolves
POST requests do not return a status code to fetch
questions.explanation: An HTTP error is still a completed exchange, so the fetch promise resolves. Keep the response and test it: if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.status).

questions.question: The browser sends `If-None-Match: "v42"` and the file has not changed. Which status code does the server send back?
questions.explanation: 304 Not Modified tells the browser its cached copy is still good, so the response has no body and the browser reuses what it stored.

questions.question: Why does a server mark its session cookie `HttpOnly`?
choices: So page JavaScript cannot read or steal it
So it is only ever sent over HTTPS
So it is deleted when the browser closes
So it is only sent with HTTP/1.1 requests
questions.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, so injected scripts cannot copy the session ID. The browser still sends it with requests. Sending only over HTTPS is the Secure attribute.

questions.question: What does it mean that HTTP is stateless, and how do sessions work around it?
questions.answer: Each request is handled on its own, with no memory of earlier requests. A session stores the user's state on the server and gives the browser a cookie holding a random session ID; the browser sends it with every request so the server can look the state up.
questions.explanation: Keeping only an unguessable ID in the cookie means the user cannot edit their own session data, and the server can end the session at any time.

questions.question: On public Wi-Fi you open `https://bank.example.com/accounts?id=7`. What can the Wi-Fi operator see?
choices: The full URL including ?id=7, but not the page content
Nothing at all, not even which server you connected to
The IP and usually the hostname, but not the path or cookies
Everything, because public Wi-Fi traffic is not covered by TLS
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts the whole HTTP message, including the path and query string. Packets still need the destination IP, and the hostname usually leaks through DNS and the TLS handshake.

questions.question: Complete the response header that lets pages on https://app.example.com read this API response.
choices: Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Request-Method
Allow
questions.explanation: Access-Control-Allow-Origin names the origin allowed to read the response. Origin is the request header the browser sends, and Access-Control-Request-Method is part of the preflight request.

questions.question: Which request best follows REST conventions for changing the email address of user 42?
choices: POST /updateUserEmail?id=42
GET /users/42/setEmail?value=new@example.com
DELETE /users/42, then POST /users with the new data
PATCH /users/42 with a JSON body containing the new email
questions.explanation: REST puts the resource in the URL and the action in the method. PATCH updates part of user 42. Changing data with GET is especially bad, because GET is supposed to be safe and may be cached or prefetched.

questions.question: A page on https://app.example.com calls https://api.example.com. The same request works in curl, but the browser console shows this. What has to change?
questions.code: Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/data' from origin 'https://app.example.com' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.
choices: The API must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin allowing https://app.example.com
The page must add an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header to its request
The page must call the API with curl instead of fetch
The API must switch from HTTPS to plain HTTP
questions.explanation: CORS permission comes from the server's response headers, and only browsers enforce it, which is why curl works. A header on the request cannot grant the page access.

questions.question: Match each part of `https://shop.example.com:8443/search?q=shoes#reviews` to its role.

pairs.right: The scheme: which protocol to use
The host: the name DNS looks up
The port: which service on the server
The path: which resource on the server
The fragment: a spot in the page, kept in the browser

questions.explanation: Reading a URL left to right gives scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment. Only the fragment never reaches the server.

questions.question: Which pair of URLs has the same origin?
choices: http://example.com/a and https://example.com/a
https://example.com/a and https://www.example.com/a
https://example.com/a and https://example.com:443/b
https://example.com/a and https://example.com:8443/a
questions.explanation: An origin is scheme plus host plus port; the path does not count. 443 is the default port for https, so the third pair is identical. The others differ in scheme, host (www is a different host) or port.

questions.question: Put the steps of resolving shop.example.com, with nothing cached, in order.
items: The OS asks its recursive resolver
The resolver asks a root server and is referred to the .com servers
A .com server refers it to example.com's authoritative name servers
The authoritative server returns the A record
The resolver caches the answer for its TTL and returns it
questions.explanation: Each server knows only the next step down the tree: root knows .com, .com knows example.com's name servers, and those hold the actual record. Caching at the end is what makes the next lookup instant.

questions.question: Match each DNS record type to what it holds.

pairs.right: A name's IPv4 address
A name's IPv6 address
An alias pointing to another name
The mail servers for a domain
Free text, such as a domain verification code

questions.explanation: A and AAAA are the address records browsers need; CNAME adds an alias step; MX is for email delivery; TXT carries verification strings and email policies.

questions.question: You moved your site to a new server and changed its A record 10 minutes ago. Some users still reach the old server. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Resolvers cached the old answer and keep using it until its TTL runs out
DNS changes only take effect after the domain is renewed
The new server must first announce itself to the root servers
Browsers look up each name only once, when they are installed
questions.explanation: Every DNS answer may be cached for its TTL. If the old record had a TTL of an hour, resolvers that fetched it recently keep serving the old IP until it expires. Lowering the TTL before a migration shortens this window.

questions.question: What does a valid TLS certificate for shop.example.com prove?
choices: That the site is safe and run by an honest business
That the server controls shop.example.com, as vouched for by a trusted CA
That nobody on the network can see which site you visit
That the server's software has no known security bugs
questions.explanation: A certificate binds a public key to a domain name, signed by a CA the browser trusts, so you know you are talking to whoever controls that domain. It says nothing about honesty or code quality, and the hostname usually still leaks through DNS and the TLS hello.

questions.question: Which of these does HTTPS protect against? Select all that apply.
choices: Someone on the same Wi-Fi reading your password as it is sent
An attacker on the network changing the page on its way to you
A server pretending to be the real site, as long as the certificate is checked
The website itself misusing the data you send it
Malware already installed on your own computer
questions.explanation: TLS gives confidentiality, integrity and server authentication for data in transit. Once the data reaches the site, or if your own machine is compromised, HTTPS cannot help.

questions.question: Type a curl command that sends a DELETE request to https://api.example.com/tasks/7.
questions.explanation: curl sends GET by default; -X (or --request) sets another method. Add -i to see the status line and headers in the output, such as 204 No Content.

questions.question: Match each HTTP method to its usual meaning in a REST API.

pairs.right: Read a resource without changing it
Create a new resource in a collection
Replace a resource completely
Change some fields of a resource
Remove a resource

questions.explanation: In REST the URL names the resource and the method is the verb. PUT and PATCH differ in scope: PUT sends the whole new version, PATCH only the changes.

questions.question: Which methods are safe, meaning they should never change data on the server? Select all that apply.
choices: GET
HEAD
POST
PUT
DELETE
OPTIONS
questions.explanation: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS only read. PUT and DELETE change data even though they are idempotent, and POST changes data and is not idempotent.

questions.question: Match each status code to its meaning.

pairs.right: Success, with no body to return
Moved for good; see the Location header
This method is not supported on this path
Too many requests; slow down
The server is temporarily unable to handle it

questions.explanation: The first digit gives the family (2 success, 3 redirect, 4 client error, 5 server error) and the rest narrows it down. 429 usually comes with a Retry-After header.

questions.question: Which response header tells the browser where to go after a 301 or 302 redirect?
questions.explanation: Redirects carry the new URL in the Location header, and the browser requests it automatically. 201 Created responses also use Location to point at the new resource.

questions.question: Your bank's session cookie is set with `SameSite=Lax`. You visit evil.example, which secretly submits a form that POSTs to bank.example/transfer. What happens?
choices: The browser sends the POST with the cookie, and the transfer succeeds
The browser blocks evil.example from sending any request to the bank
The bank detects an HttpOnly violation and logs you out
The POST goes out without the session cookie, so the bank sees no login
questions.explanation: SameSite=Lax withholds the cookie from cross-site POSTs (it still sends it when you follow a normal link with GET). The request itself is sent, but without your session it cannot act as you. Banks add CSRF tokens as a second layer.

questions.question: A security review flags the session cookie in this login response. Which change fixes the real problems?
questions.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Set-Cookie: session=8f2a9c41e7b04d; Path=/
choices: Add HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax to the cookie
Rename the cookie so attackers cannot guess its name
Store the username in the cookie instead of an ID
Add Max-Age=31536000 so users stay logged in
questions.explanation: Without HttpOnly an injected script can read the session ID, without Secure it could travel over plain HTTP, and without SameSite other sites can trigger requests that carry it. The cookie name was never the secret.

questions.question: A mobile app sends `Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...` with each API call. How does this differ from a session cookie?
choices: The token is encrypted by HTTP itself, while cookies travel in plain text
Tokens only work over HTTP/2, while cookies work with every version
The app attaches the token itself; nothing sends it automatically like a cookie
The server must store every token, while cookies need no server storage
questions.explanation: Cookies are attached by the browser on every matching request, which is what makes CSRF possible. A bearer token is added by the app's own code. Both rely on HTTPS for encryption, and signed tokens such as JWTs often need no server-side storage at all.

questions.question: Why do sites name built files like `app.3f9c2b.js` and serve them with `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`?
choices: The hash hides the source code from people reading the page
Browsers can cache them for a year, and a new release gets a new name, so updates still arrive
Long file names make the CDN compress the files more aggressively
The hash lets the browser skip the TLS certificate check
questions.explanation: The name changes whenever the content changes, so a cached file can never be stale: new HTML simply references a new URL. That makes year-long caching safe and saves a request per file on every visit.

questions.question: You visited shop.example.com a minute ago. On your next visit, which steps are usually skipped or shortened? Select all that apply.
choices: The DNS lookup, because the answer is cached
The TCP and TLS handshakes, if the connection is still open
Downloading fingerprinted assets, which come from the cache
Sending an HTTP request for the HTML page
Parsing and rendering the HTML
questions.explanation: Caches and open connections remove whole steps. The HTML is usually served with no-cache, so the browser still asks for it (perhaps getting a 304), and the page must always be parsed and rendered again.
